cells.tense: The structure has come down, and you are letting the opening stay open instead of rushing to name it.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Give a small daily bit of attention to what the clearing brought out — a habit that no longer fits, a question nobody has asked yet — without making it become anything.
cells.core:
You can stay in a clearing without pinning it down. A role, a plan, a version of events you kept feeding has stopped holding, and instead of rushing to build a replacement, you're letting it be open. Your mind is fresh there, turning the pieces over with a patience most people lose when their structures go.

So keep it fed, a little at a time. Give some daily attention to what the clearing brought out — a habit that no longer fits, a question nobody has asked. Don't ask it to become an answer. What you have is an eye for what's real before it takes a shape. Feeding that daily is how the next thing shows itself without you forcing the plan.
cells.sheetLine: You can stand in what came loose without rushing a wall back up.
cells.verb: meeting what is real in the opening with fresh attention
cells.place: where a structure built on something untrue has just given way

cells.tense: You are already building the replacement before the old structure has finished coming down.
cells.act: tend the small thing and learn from it
cells.ask: Keep up something you already do — a plant, a practice, a daily task — through this week, and watch what it asks of you before you decide what it means.
cells.core:
The next shelter is going up in your head before the old one has finished falling. Every loose piece gets a sturdier replacement designed around it, and the design was not asked for. It looks like strength from inside. From the outside, it looks like someone laying bricks at a site that hasn't finished emptying.

So don't finish emptying it faster. Keep up something you already do — a plant, a practice, an actual task — and hold it simply. See what it asks of you before deciding what it means or what it becomes. Tending that slows the whole manager down, and the clearing gets room to finish the sentence it started.

cells.tense: The clearing happened, and you are still describing it as if it hasn't, still at the door it left behind.
cells.act: follow a raw curiosity with no use for it
cells.ask: Follow something you actually want to know — a subject, a question, a place — with no plan for what it's for, and stop where it stops.
cells.core:
You're in the after, not the before. Something loosened, and your account still places you in the old place. You're describing what you are doing there long after the walls came down, and the description is costing you the new ground. The curiosity that would sort this out is sitting unspent.

Follow something you actually want to know, with nothing to gain from it. A subject, a question, a place you've meant to look into. Go as far as it goes and stop where it stops. This isn't analysis — it's what your mind does when you stop feeding it the old account. Real curiosity is enough to rebuild contact with what is actually here. It spends only the time you were already using on the old description.

cells.tense: The space is being kept clear by your hand, and if asked you would say you haven't touched it.
cells.act: put the inquiry on paper and follow it
cells.ask: Write out what is actually gone, in order, no feeling words, just the facts of what was there and what isn't. Then follow it wherever it leads.
cells.core:
You don't see yourself in the clearing. From inside, it looks like something that occurred — an event with no author. But the shape of it carries your fingerprints: the way you've let one version go and kept another, the order things have come loose. Someone is holding the space open, quietly, without claiming it. That is not a small thing, and it isn't happening by accident.

Put it on paper. Write what is actually gone, in order, plain facts, no mood, no story. Then read it back. This is the work of getting your hands back onto what you have been doing. Not to tighten up — to know it was your work, and to have the record there when you wonder.
cells.sheetLine: You're authoring the clearing and calling it none of your doing.
